GARHWALI.
Garhwal, as a tract, consists of two portions, viz., the State of Tehri Garhwal, and,
to its east, the British District of Garhwal. This tract is
bounded on the west by the Jaunsir-Bawar tract of Dehra
Dun, the language of which is the Western Pahari Jaunsari, and on the east by the
Almora District of Kumaun, the main language-of which is Kumauni. To its north
are the higher ranges of the Himalaya, inhabited by people speaking Tibeto-Burman
forms of speech which are dealt with in Vol. TIT, Part T, of this Survey, and to its south
are the British Districts of Dehra Dun and (again) Almora. Still further south lie the
Districts of Saharanpur, Bijnor and Moradabad, of which, and also of most of Dehra Dun,
the language is some form of Western Hindi. Garhwali is the Aryan language spoken
in Garhwal, and also to some extent by an overflow population in all the above adjoining
districts. 4
As previously explained (ante, pp. 13 ff.) Garhwal atan carly period received Aryan
‘Colonies from Rajputana, using that name in its widest sense. The founder of the
present line of rulers of Tehri is said to have boon a Pala immigrant from Gujarat, who
is differently named in the various lists. According to some he was no other than the
famous Kanishka.' Thirty-sixth or thirty-seventh in descent from the founder came
Ajaya Pala, who lived in the latter half of the fourteenth century A.D. He consolidated
the power of his family over the other tribes in Garhwal, and transferred his capital to
Srinagar, the present chief town of the British District. Up to his time Garhwal had
Deen divided amongst a number of pelty Rajas. “ Every glen or hill, as formerly was
the case in the highlands of Scotland, was subject to its own chiefs who have left no
record behind except the moss-covered walls of their strongholds. And, although Ajaya
Pala is credited with having reduced fifty-two of these petty chiefs under his own rules,
we may well suppose that he was only the first of his line to aim at more than a local
supremacy, and that to his successors is due the extension of the Garhwal power over
the Dun, Bisahir (Bashahy) and the tract now known as Tehri or foreign Garhwal.’””
Besides Tiboto-Burmans tho lower ranges of the Himalaya from the Jehlam to Nepal
were inhabited by various Aryan tribes, the principal of which was that of the Khagas.’
Those of Garhwal were subdued by these Rajput conquerors, and adopted their Jan-
guage, infecting it, at the same time, with idioms belonging to their own form of speech.
It thus follows that Gayhwali is asomewhat corrupted form of Rajasthani. This corruption
‘is not so manifest as itis in the Western Pahari languages of the Simla Hills, further
west, but here and there we come across forms of words which distinctly betray Khasa
influence. This subject will be dealt with more fully, when considering the Simla and
allied dialects. .
Garhwali is closely allied to Kumauni. Its Rajasthani zelationship is clear to
the most casual observer, and need not detain us further.
Garhwali is not a literary language, and in the. mountainous tract that forms its
home, it is to be expected that it should change from place
to.place. No less than. eight varieties have been reported

The principal forms of Garhwali Grammar are given in Dr. Kellogg’s Hinds
Kibcsiaas Grammar (2nd edition, London, 1893). No other book
with which the writer is acquainted deals with the gram~-
matical forms of this dialect. Pandit Ganga Datt Upreti’s specimens have been referred
to above.
A sketch of Garhwali Grammar.
The following sketeh of Garhwali Grammar is based on the two specimens given
below, on the list of words and sentences on pp. 353 and ff. and, when material was not
there available, on a Garhwali version of the Gospel of St. Matthew printed at Lucknow
in 1876. The quotations from the first specimen (the Parable of the Prodigal Son}
and from the List of Words and Sentences will readily be recognized, and no references.
are added to them. ‘The paragraphs of the second specimen, which is taken from Pandit
Ganga Datt Upreti’s Hill Dialects of the Rumaun Division, have been numbered.
All quotations taken from it, and from the version of St. Matthew’s Gospel, are supplied
with references.
Pronunciation.—The pronunciation is on the whole the same asin Hindi. I
have not noticed any instance of the interchange between yé and @ which is a promi-
nent feature in Kumeuni. Words which in Hindi ond in é,in Garhwali often ond in
ashort unpronounced a. Thus the postposition of the Agent case is » (Hindi né), the
suffix of the conjunctive participle is 4 (Hindi 4a), and the oblique form of the infinitive
in phrases is as in karan lagyd (Hindi karné lag@). Although Garhwili is distinctively
aform of Eastern Rajasthani, we may say that in its general characteristics it more
nearly approaches Hindi than does Kumauni or Khas-Kuri.
Gender.—There are two genders, masculine and feminine. These generally follow
Hindi and ‘Rajasthani rules. A few words which are feminine in Hindi are, as in
-Kumauni, masculine in Garhwali. Thus, 2&0, an eye, is masculine in méré akha té
khar nikalt-dé, extract the grass from my eye (II, 4).
Number.—There are two numbers, singular and plural. “Zadbhava' masculine
nouns which in Hindi end in 4, in Garhwali, as in Rajasthani, end in 6. Thus, Hindi
ghora, Garhwali ghdrd, a horse. These nouns form the nominative plural by changing
6 to Gas in ghara, horses.
In the case of other masculine nouns, the nominative plural is the same as the
nominative singular. Thus, ghar,a house, or houses. *
Feminine nouns ending in consonants form the nominative plural by adding a.
Thus, bat, a word, bata (Hindi bat#), words, In the case of other feminine nouns the
nominative plural is the same as the nominative singular. Thus, naunz, a daughter or
daughters. Feminine nouns in 2, however, often change the z to é in the nominative
plual. Thus, jandnz, a woman, plural janéne or janine.
Case.—As in other Indo-Aryan languages, cases are generally indicated by means.
‘wf postpositions. Certain nouns are put into an oblique form before these are added.
In the case of most nouns the oblique form singular is the same as the nominative,
Thus, bir, a hero: bir-an, by the hero: ghar, a house: ghar-t8, from a house : naunt»
1a tadbhava noun is one which lasdescended to Garhwall from Sanskrit through Prakrit, and which is nob (like
blak, a boy) borrowed direstly from Sanskrit.

The Genitive governed by pas is sometimes used after a vorb of speaking, although
the Locative with ma is the most usual idiom. ‘Thus :—
wai-n wai-ké pds bolyd, he said to him (thysbrother is come).
As examples of the Locative we have:—

apea khétiema bhéjyo, he sent him into his fields.
gala-par lipti-k chimyo, clinging on. his neck, he kissed (him).
Wa sometimes means ‘on’ and par ‘in.’ Thus:—
we-ki pithma kathi dhar, put the saddle on his back.
méro baba wé chhité ghar-par rahddin, my father lives in that small house.
After a verb of speaking the regular form is the Locative with md, as in chhé
nawnydl-an apna baba-jt-mé bole, the younger son said to his father. See, however, the
Dative and the Genitive.
“ From-among” is ma-n, as in mai-sant apua naukari-md-» ék-kd barabar bandud,
make me as one from among your servants.
Adjectives.—-Except tadbhava adjectives in 6, all adjectives are immutable.
Tadbhava adjectives in 6 change the termination to z when agreeing with a feminine
noun. When agreeing with a masculine noun in the plural or in any case of the
singular except the nominative (including the accusative when the same in form as the
nominative) the 6 is changed to a. Thus :—
dhalé ddmi, a good man.
bhalé ddma, good men.
bhald admi-ko, of a good man.
bhali Janina, a. good woman.
bhala janint, good women.
Comparison is made, as usual, by putting the thing with which comparison is
made in the ablative case. Examples are given above under the head of the ablative.

ék pakaryé jalz, one (woman) will be seized (Matt. xxiv, 41).
In Kumauni there is an organic Passive formed by adding 7 to the root. I have
met one or two examples of a corresponding form in Garhwali, in :-—
86 swarg-ma khéliya rald, that will remain loosed in heaven (Matt. xviii, 18).
ké-té lunid karilo, wherewith will it be made salted (Matt. v, 13)?
Causal verbs are formed as in Hindi by adding d to the root. The infinitive ends
in aund. Thus, charaund, past participle chardyd, to cause to graze.
There are numerous irregular causal verbs. Most of these also follow Hindi; eg.
marnd, to die; marnd, to kill. We have an example of the Causal of khénd, to
eat, in:—
sini khaawnd, Hoe fecdeth them (Matt. vi, 26).
Compound verbs are formed much as in Hindi. Examples are :—
Intensiv
dé-déwa, give away: Dat-diyé, he divided ; chati-gayd, he went away,
Potentials —
mi-kis sapha kart sakdé, Thou canst make me clean (Matt. viii, 2).
kui nt bole sakyd, no one could speak (Matt. xxii, 46).
Completives :—
jub 6 sab urée chuké, when he had finished squandering everything.
Desideratives :-—
Bhitar jand nz chayd, he did not wish to go inside.
Ineoptiv
6 Gnand karan lagyo, he began to rejoice. See also under the head of the
Infinitive.
Permissive :—
mary apna maryaii-kis khadyawn dé, let the dead bury their dead (Matt.
viii, 22),
Thave not noted an instance of an Aequisitive compound.
The ordinary Negative is ni, of which numerous examples will be found in the
specimens. We also sometimes find na, as in examples on pp. 208 and 295. With the
imperative we have né, as in bhitre-té kichhu chie-bast lép-ki ni wtar, let him not
descend to take any property from within (Matt, xxiv, 17).

greater parts of the Chandpur and Dewalgarh Parganas, and also in about thirty villages

pretend to be a complete grammar, and most attention will be devoted to those points
in which the dialect differs from Standard Garhwali.

is the case with the Standard dialect. The vowel é is interchangeable with ya; thus we
have both dyé and dé, give, and dyas, dés, a country. When é is followed in the

This dialect is spoken in Dasauli Pargana, and in the adjoining parts of Painkhanda
Pargana of British Garhwal, by an estimated number of 17,022 people.

tion. This will be evident from the short extract from the Parable of the Prodigal Son.
annexed. Comparison will show that it differs from Badhani principally in preferring
the present participle in do to that in 20, but even this may be a matter of personal equa-
tion of the writers of the two versions. We may note the past tense in 16 of a passive
formed by adding #, in the word nathiyaiyald, had been squandered. Note also the word

verb kahnd, to say, (quasi, he said for eating), but I am not certain as to the form. We
may also note that the oblique plural ends in ai and & (@) instead of the Bathani 3, but
this also may be merely a matter of spelling.

folk-tale in that dialect on pp. 78 and ff. of Pandit Ganga Dutt Upréti’s Hill Dialects
of the Kumaun Division.

NAGPURIYA.
This dialect is spoken in the Nagpur Pargana, and in the adjoining parts of Pargana
Painkhanda in tho north-west of British Garhwal, by an estimated number of 51,881
people. It is not really a separate dialect, being practically the same as Dasaulya
and Majh-Kumaiyi.. This will be evident from the extract from the Parable of the
Prodigal Son given below.

word baikh, a corruption of békat or békti, a person: of sé as a postposition of the
ablative ; and of the oblique plural in @ in nawkri.

not dphi. As in Dasaulya, the present participle in mdo appears, as well as that in nd.
We find the Kumauni future in jaa and bala, and the common change of final é to a in
dina. Note the past tense in ala in wrayalé.

SALANT.
With Nagpuriya we conclude our survey of the Aryan dialects of the north of
British Garhwal. Further north still we come upon a number of forms of Tibetan de-
scribed in Vol. III, Part I of this Survey, pp. 100 ff. Over the Southern Parganas of
the district, south of the Rathi dialect, we come to Salini, named after the three
Parganas of Malla, Talli, and Ganga Salin. The dialect is also spoken in the
Parganas immediately to the north of the three Salins, and in the western portion of.
Pargana Pali of Almora. Garhwali is also reported from the neighbouring districts of
Dehra Dun, Saharanpur, Bijuor, and Moradabad, and we may assume that here also it
is spoken in the form of Salani.
The estimated number of speakers is therefore :—

Saldni is practically the same as Srinagariya, the standard form of Garhwali. This
will be evident from the version of the Parable of the Prodigal Son annexed.
The only differences to be noted are the following. In the Standard dialect, words
which in Hindi end in é¢, end in a short unpronounced a. In Salani, to judge from the
spelling of all the specimens received, this final « is pronounced, so that the postposition
of the agent case is za, not 2, and the suffix of the conjunctive participle is ka, not k.
It will be remembered that the samo ocours in all the other dialects of Garhwili.
Another example of this tendency to pronounce a final a is in the word kuchha, any-
thing, Standard Zuchh. In tho verb substantive we have cha as well as chha for ‘he is?
a change which also occurs in other dialects.
The only new form which occurs in the specimen is fdndéna, becoming, in the
passage where the son remembers that his father’s servants used to get much bread
toeat. A similar form will be met in the Tehri dialect,

B42
TEHRI GARHWALI OR GANGAPARIYA.
The State of Tehri Garhwal lies to the west of British Garhwal, from which it is sopar-
ated along the southern portion of its boundary by the river Ganges. Its language is a
recognised dialect of Garhwali, known as the Tehri dialect, and also by people of Garh-
wal and Almora, as “ Gaigapariyi” or the language of the country beyond the Ganges.
The number of speakers is estimated at 240,281.
Immediately to the west of the Tehri State lies the Jaunsir-Bawar tract of the
District of Dehra Dun, the language of which is the Western Pahari Jaunsari. As
might be expected, the Tehri dialect shows distinet traces of the latter form of speech,
the most important of which is the frequent use of the word dhayé instead of chhayd,
to mean ‘was.’ Compare the Jaunsari thd.
It is reported that the dialect varies from place to place over the whole State. This
is'to be expected. The specimens given below represent: the form of speech current in
the neighbourhood of Tehri, the chief town of the State. The specimens consist of a
version of the Parable of the Prodigal Son, and of a well-known folk-tale,—tho fable of
the Bundle of Sticks. Another (and excellent) example will be found on pp. 66 and
ff. of Pandit Ganga Datt Uprati’s Hill Dialects of the Kumaun Division.
Tt is unnecessary to give a complete sketch of the grammar of Tehri Garhwali. It
will be sufficient to note the principal points of divergence ‘from the Standard dialect.
Nouns.—The principal postpositions are :—
Agent, na.
Dative-Accusative, hi, ka, sant ; for, lda.
Instrumental, na, sé, #2.
Ablative, mujé, sé, té ; from among, mé-na.
Genitive, hd (ha, hi).
Locative, ma, mit.
The locative postpositions are used after verbs of saying, like the Standard md.
Substantives and adjectives make their oblique forms as in the Standard. The
plural oblique terminations are aw and &, both of which are frequently nasalized. ‘Thus,
bitbau-ko or bibaii-ko, of fathers; mansii-k6 or mansii-kd, of men.
Adjectives follow the same rules as in the Standard. For ‘one’ the word bar gat
(ie. barkad, good luck) is usually employed in counting.
Pronouns closcly follow the Standard. The usual oblique form of fa, thou, is twai,
as in twai-na (ag. sing.). Similarly, the agent singular of maf, I, is mai-na ov mai-na.
For yé, this, he, and wé, that, he, we have :—
This, he, she, it. That, he, she, it.
‘Maso, Fem, Singular. Maso. Fem.
Nom. yo ye wd, wa, wa
Obl. ya yai yf 106, wai oF
Plural.
Nom. yé, yo wo, a (a)
Obl. yaw (ya, yis (yit) a (@)
Gen. inaré, yii-kd unas, H-k5
The Reflexive Pronoun is aphi, self; genitive apyd. Aphi-ma is “amongst
themselves.” a
